chapter: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
title: King Oliver's 1923 Chicago band and the two-cornet breaks
summary: Rose says the 1923 band fit the form only some of the time. Two cornets were unusual indoors in New Orleans, and Oliver signalled Louis Armstrong's breaks by fingering the valves.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Is the, uh, the King Oliver Creole Band of 1923 that played in Chicago, is, does that fit the, uh, description, uh, of a jazz ensemble band?

I would say that it, that it frequently fits the description, but not, not all the time. Uh, by the time you had Oliver in New Orleans, in Chicago, uh, you already had a set band for one thing, which had the opportunity to play a location job for a long period of time. Mm-hmm. And to, uh, to some extent to work out, uh, not exactly arrangements, but to work out, uh, uh, common activities, musically, on the stand. And, uh, of course, you also had, uh, a certain increase in the amount of solo play, which, of course, is very little in the King Oliver Band of 1923, but more than it would have been in New Orleans. Uh, uh, uh, uh, the, uh, uh, sort of anomaly, uh, present in the fact that you had two horns, two cornets playing together in that band, which was something that did not happen indoors in New Orleans. Indoors, but in a parade. In a parade, you would have it. In a brass band, you might have one. You would have two or three. You have two or three. But you see, in, indoors, uh, that was virtually unknown to have two cornets playing. So, uh, uh, why did Oliver
Well, uh, he did it, he did it, uh, to some extent to make more noise. He did it to some extent because of the fact that there was a certain joy and satisfaction in playing along.

But from a formal standpoint, there was no necessity for that. He was also following certain trends that had come into existence by that time of having larger augmented orchestras, and he felt the need of having some kind of a show on the stage, feeling that too small a group didn't look right.
Now, those coronet breaks that Louis and Joel did together, they were rehearsed, were they?

No, they weren't rehearsed, but I would say that the principle on which they were done were well-established between them. And the way it worked was that Oliver would signal the break that he was going to make to Louis by fingering the valves on his cornet, and Louis could immediately see what it was that he was going to do. And so when the break came, they would have these miraculous, and there's nothing short of that, two cornet breaks. Of course, jazz fans ever since have appreciated what took place on those sessions.
